item.title: Chinese defense firm introduces 40mm cased telescoped ammunition, already fielded by multiple domestic platforms
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27 22:41:00
Type 100 support vehicles are reviewed at China's V-Day military parade on September 3, 2025. Photo: Screenshot from Changan Wangjiang A new Chinese 40mm cased telescoped ammunition round can punch through 130 millimeters of homogeneous steel armor from a kilometer away - firepower that leaves conventional shells far behind - while offering three damage modes: armor-piercing, high-explosive fragmentation and programmable airburst. The round is already being used by multiple domestic weapons platforms, a Chinese state-owned defense company said on Monday, while providing footage showing the Type 100 support vehicles and new-generation airborne combat vehicles that debuted during the 2025 V-Day military parade. The projectile of the telescoped ammunition is enclosed inside the cartridge case, making the entire round a single cylinder. A single shot can punch through 130 millimeters of homogeneous steel armor, and easily deal with field fortifications and low, slow and small (LSS) aerial targets, said Changan Wangjiang, a defense company under the China South Industries Group, in a video released on its official social media account on WeChat on Monday. An ammunition storage box inside a vehicle armed with domestic 40mm cased telescoped rounds Photo: Screenshot from Changan Wangjiang The round uses a disruptive two-stage ignition design: the first ignition separates the projectile structure and drives the projectile into a locked position, letting the cartridge case form a sealed chamber. A second ignition then sends the round flying at meteoric speed, giving the cased telescoped ammunition its formidable striking power. The round also uses a dart-like aerodynamic layout and fin stabilization, achieving accuracy of 0.5 meters by 0.5 meters at one kilometer, making it not only powerful, but precise enough for near-perfect hits. The 40mm round currently has three main damage modes. The round's first damage mode is the armor penetration mode. Able to punch through 130mm of steel plate from a kilometer away, it can seriously damage main battle tanks. Its second mode, high-explosive fragmentation, sends blast waves in all directions upon impact. Just a few rounds can destroy fortifications and bunkers. The third, programmable airburst, detonates the shell midair to form a dense barrage that leaves drones and other low-slow-small aerial targets nowhere to hide. Cased telescoped ammunition is not new, the concept has existed for years. China pursued it for several reasons, Chinese military affairs expert Song Zhongping told the Global Times. First, tanks and armored vehicles have limited internal space, so cased telescoped rounds allow more ammunition to be carried. Second, they hold more propellant, giving greater striking power. They also generate relatively low recoil and have a neat, regular shape that makes transport easier. The 40mm round is already being used with multiple domestically produced weapons, achieving seamless coverage across all terrains and time periods, a development set to begin a new era of smarter, more efficient Chinese equipment, according to Changan Wangjiang. The information about the new round accompanied footage of Type 100 support vehicles and new-generation domestic airborne combat vehicles, both of which debuted at the V-Day military parade held in Beijing on September 3, 2025. The Type 100 support vehicle can collaborate with the Type 100 tank. While the tank's main gun has strong firepower, the tank faces challenges in engaging multiple targets simultaneously. This is when the fire support vehicle comes in, using its higher rate of fire to suppress and eliminate unarmored targets such as foot soldiers operating anti-tank missiles or lightly armored vehicles, an expert told the Global Times in a previous interview. Airborne combat vehicles can be transported across long distances via the air and provide heavily armored mobile support. They act as the airborne edges in the PLA's fast response and deep strike operations. The large-scale fielding of specially improved conventional munitions shows that the PLA's overall ammunition design philosophy is becoming more forward-looking and more efficient, Song added.

item.title: Philippines claims the Liaoning carrier group transited waters off Mindanao; expert says passage shows routine training with growing tactical flexibility
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27 18:31:00
The Liaoning aircraft carrier participates in a dual-aircraft-carrier formation drill on October 21, 2024. Photo: VCG The Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Navy Liaoning carrier task group, currently training in relevant waters of the Western Pacific, was spotted passing through waters off Mindanao last week, the Armed Forces of the Philippines' (AFP) Western Mindanao Command (WestMinCom) claimed on Monday, according to Philippine media INQUIRER.net. This is likely the second time the Liaoning has transited the central Philippine maritime region, after a memorable passage in 2024, a Chinese military affairs expert said, adding that the tactical value lies in the route planning, and that this successful maneuver shows the Liaoning 's far-sea training has brought a wider range of sea lanes into its routine scope. In a statement, WestMinCom claimed its Maritime Situational Awareness Center and other maritime units tracked the Liaoning group as it transited the Zamboanga Peninsula region last Thursday, INQUIRER.net said. Military tracking initially spotted the aircraft carrier fleet northwest of Talulu Point in Siocon, Zamboanga del Norte. The fleet was later monitored southwest of Maitum, Sarangani, as it moved southeastward toward the Celebes Sea, INQUIRER.net claimed. Wang Yunfei, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times that this is likely the Liaoning 's second transit through the central Philippine maritime region. The last time was in October 2024, when the carrier group took a route that seems to have left a deep impression on many. This time, Wang said, the carrier group chose a relatively less-used waterway south of the Philippines instead, with its tactical value lying in the route planning. He noted that the move is consistent with international law and practices. The first practical benefit is avoiding typhoons. A typhoon is currently forming in the Western Pacific, and strong winds and huge waves would severely limit carrier aircraft takeoffs, landings and formation sailing, conditions that are less than ideal for normal training. The waters off south-central Philippines, sheltered by Mindanao and the Sulu Archipelago, offer a natural barrier with much more stable conditions. Choosing this route effectively sidesteps the typhoon zone, ensuring the formation can maintain its training rhythm without being forced to interrupt operations due to bad weather. Second, Wang noted that the route allows another approach into the Western Pacific, with a heading relatively close to Guam, the core hub base for US forces on the second island chain, and a key node for force dispatch, logistics and long-range projection. "In the past, Chinese carriers entering the Western Pacific mostly took the Miyako Strait to the north or the Bashi Channel in the middle, which was easier for Japanese and US reconnaissance to track them continuously and predict their course in advance. Going through the southern Philippines amounts to a new entry channel, making it more challenging for the outside world to predict the direction of operations. Once through these waters and heading east, the formation can directly approach the open Western Pacific near Guam for training," Wang said. The expert also said that a carrier group's long voyage is not simply a show of presence. Far-sea maneuvering itself is the most important part of training. A carrier tests not only whether carrier aircraft can take off, but the entire set of capabilities for navigation, formation coordination, replenishment and concealed maneuvering in unfamiliar waters and complex island and reef channels. Narrow straits, underwater currents, dense islands and reefs, as well as complex electromagnetic environments make for excellent natural training grounds. This maneuver was a highly successful tactical move, Wang said. It shows the outside world that Chinese carriers entering the Western Pacific do not have just two or three fixed routes to choose from. The track also sends a clear signal: the Liaoning 's far-sea training is routine and systematic, not a one-off short cruise, he said. Having passed through the central Philippine maritime region in 2024 and again two years later, the navy has brought this far-sea channel into its routine route planning, familiarizing itself with local sea conditions, hydrology and the electromagnetic environment. This reflects the growing maturity of the PLA Navy's ocean-going planning, able to advance and withdraw freely, maneuver flexibly and steadily hone far-sea combat capability across the vast Western Pacific. On October 14, China's Ministry of National Defense announced that the PLA Navy had organized the Liaoning carrier group to conduct training in relevant waters of the Western Pacific that day. It was a routine training mission under the annual plan, aimed at testing and improving combat-oriented training and continuously enhancing the ability to fulfill missions. It complies with relevant international law and practice and does not target any specific country or target.

item.title: US intelligence hypes Chinese, Russian space threats while accelerating its own military buildup in orbit
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27 15:08:00
Militarizing space. Illustration: Chen Xia/GT Like Don Quixote tilting at windmills he mistook for menacing giants, Washington appears to be sounding the alarm over alleged threats in outer space, even as it presses ahead with its own military buildup in orbit. In its latest assessment, released on Monday, the US Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) claimed that China could deploy space-based directed-energy weapons by the late 2020s, while also highlighting Russia's expanding anti-satellite capabilities, according to SpaceNews. However, the claims come even as the US itself accelerates the militarization of outer space, having already publicly acknowledged deploying weapons in orbit while advancing its ambitious Golden Dome missile defense initiative. Chinese military affairs expert Song Zhongping told the Global Times that Washington's approach represents a classic case of "thief crying stop the thief," as the US seeks to justify its own buildup of offensive and defensive space capabilities by portraying China and Russia as threats. According to SpaceNews, the DIA's latest assessment, contained in the 2026 edition of Challenges to Security in Space, claimed that China already possesses multiple ground-based laser systems capable of disrupting, degrading or damaging satellites in low-Earth orbit. The report further alleged that Beijing may field space-based directed-energy weapons by the late 2020s, along with more powerful ground-based systems capable of threatening satellites in orbit. Directed-energy weapons use concentrated electromagnetic energy, including lasers and high-powered microwaves, to interfere with or damage targets. Such systems could potentially disrupt satellite electronics or impair optical sensors, according to SpaceNews. The US intelligence report also highlighted Russia's alleged development of kinetic anti-satellite weapons, including the Burevestnik system, which it described as a developmental co-orbital anti-satellite weapon launched from a modified MiG-31 aircraft. It further reiterated Washington's assessment that Moscow is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon. Moscow has said that Cosmos 2553, a satellite linked by US intelligence to the alleged program, was intended to test electronic systems under radiation conditions. Song said the latest US intelligence assessment reveals two distinct strategic calculations behind Washington's claims against China and Russia. By hyping China's potential development of space-based weapons, the US is seeking to justify its own deployment of offensive weapons in orbit, while claims about Russia's anti-satellite capabilities aim to make the case for strengthening the defenses of American space assets, Song noted. Such claims could also help the US administration secure additional congressional funding for an integrated space warfare architecture combining offensive and defensive capabilities, he said. Notably, the latest allegations stand against the backdrop of Washington's increasingly explicit pursuit of military capabilities in space. On September 14, US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink publicly acknowledged that the US already possessed on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending its military forces against hostile actions. The announcement marked a significant development in Washington's public posture toward space warfare, although the US military did not disclose the specific capabilities, the number deployed or their deployment dates. Meanwhile, Washington is pressing ahead with its Golden Dome missile defense initiative, which includes the development of a constellation of space-based interceptors. According to an official US Space Force release in July, the program aims to develop interceptors capable of engaging missiles during their boost, midcourse and glide phases. According to an official US Space Force release in April, the service has established the Space-Based Interceptor (SBI) program to develop a space-based missile defense system, with plans to demonstrate its integration into the Golden Dome architecture by 2028. Song noted that the US is increasingly seeking to transform outer space from a domain used primarily to support military operations through reconnaissance, communications and navigation into a domain for direct offensive and defensive operations. He said Washington's pursuit of space-based weapons, including capabilities envisioned under the Golden Dome initiative, reflects its broader ambition to maintain military superiority by integrating advanced technologies and extending military operations into space. China, meanwhile, has repeatedly called for efforts to prevent an arms race in outer space and opposed attempts to turn it into a battlefield. In its latest position paper titled China's Position on Strengthening Outer Space Governance, released on October 23, the Chinese Foreign Ministry warned: "The risk of an arms race in outer space and the trend of turning outer space into a new theater of conflict have become the gravest threat and challenge to space security." The document further stated: "States should oppose offensive military policies in outer space and take all possible measures to prevent an arms race in outer space." Song warned that Washington's push to integrate artificial intelligence into military systems and expand offensive and defensive capabilities into space could transform outer space from a domain supporting military operations into a battlefield, threatening other countries' space assets and potentially accelerating an arms race and increasing the risk of conflicts triggered by miscalculation, he said.

item.title: China, Indonesia to hold 'Sharp Knife' joint exercise after 14-year hiatus; focus on mountainous hostage-rescue operations, manned-unmanned coordination
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26 21:22:00
Photo: VCG From late October to early November, the Chinese and Indonesian militaries will hold the "Sharp Knife 2026" army counter-terrorism joint training exercise in South China's Guangdong Province, China's Ministry of National Defense (MND) announced on Monday. This marks the third iteration of this series and the first in 14 years. A military affairs expert told the Global Times that the exercise falls under non-traditional security cooperation, with both sides restarting the mechanism to jointly combat transnational and local crime and eliminate major risks posed by terrorism. The training this year takes on joint mountain counter-terrorism rescue operations with a focus on mountain climbing, special vehicle driving, helicopter rappelling, close-quarters assault and manned-unmanned coordination, according to the MND. This is the third time the two sides have held this series of joint exercises, which will help deepen practical exchanges and cooperation between the two militaries and improve their joint operational capabilities, the MND said. Song Zhongping, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times that this amounts to a set of special operations procedures for hostage rescue in a dense, mountainous forest environment: drones conduct reconnaissance first, ground teams climb and use special vehicles to maneuver and seal off the area, helicopters rappel in vertically, and finally close-quarters indoor assaults identify and free hostages. The focus is on dealing with armed hostage-taking strongholds entrenched in mountainous areas. "It looks like hardcore special operations, but this is non-traditional security cooperation. On one hand, it fills gaps in both sides' tactical capabilities for joint operations in complex mountain environments; on the other, it continues to strengthen security coordination with ASEAN countries and serves regional governance needs such as counter-fraud and counter-human trafficking," Song said. In June 2011, the China-Indonesia "Sharp Knife 2011" special forces joint training exercise was held in Bandung, Indonesia. The first joint training was aimed at consolidating friendship, enhancing mutual understanding and trust, promoting practical exchanges and cooperation, and improving counter-terrorism capabilities. In July 2012, the two militaries' special forces held "Sharp Knife 2012" in Jinan, East China's Shandong Province. As the second special forces joint training between the two countries, it aimed to consolidate the results of the first drill. With the series restarting after 14 years, Song said that "Sharp Knife" carries important practical significance. "Indonesia faces both external and homegrown terrorism risks, which is an important reason it needs to strengthen counter-terrorism and non-traditional security drills. At the same time, cross-border telecom fraud, human trafficking and cross-border movement of illicit assets are all key areas where China and Indonesia need to cooperate," the expert said. On one hand, China is also a victim of telecom fraud and needs to cooperate with Southeast Asian countries including Indonesia; on the other, Indonesia needs China's mature counter-terrorism experience, Song added. Notably, since 2025, the Ministerial Meeting of China-Indonesia Joint Foreign and Defense Ministerial Dialogue has convened twice. The dialogue is the first ministerial-level "2+2" mechanism China has established globally, providing a new platform for strategic communication between the two countries. In August, Indonesian Defense Minister Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin said at the second meeting that Indonesia is ready to strengthen strategic communication with China, enhance exchanges between the two militaries, and deepen cooperation in areas including defense, maritime security, cybersecurity, online gambling and telecommunications fraud, as well as transnational crime, Xinhua reported. Indonesia sits in the Malacca region, and counter-terrorism, counter-piracy and humanitarian assistance are all important areas of China-Indonesia cooperation, Song said. "Cooperation between the PLA and the Indonesian military is about restarting the relevant mechanisms, sharing information and jointly combating transnational and local crime to eliminate major risks posed by terrorism," he added.

item.title: Four early warning aircraft based on Y-20 platform seen in Chinese factory on satellite imagery; foreign media speculates on serial production
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-25 22:22:00
Y-20B large transport aircraft sit on the tarmac. File photo: Official WeChat account of China Bugle Citing new satellite imagery, a foreign media report claims that four of China's new KJ-3000 airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft, also referred to as the KJ-20, have been seen in a Chinese aircraft production facility. The report further speculated that the large radar planes, which are based on the four-engine Y-20 transport aircraft, are moving toward or have entered serial production. Chinese experts have also long expected an early warning variant of the Y-20. The report by US media outlet The War Zone (TWZ) on Thursday noted that the new aircraft features a large circular radome mounted above the rear fuselage, along with a prominent series of antennas on the forward fuselage. An aerial refueling probe is mounted above the cockpit, while a conspicuous intake at the base of the tailfin is likely intended to provide cooling air for its extensive onboard electronics. Citing an analyst, the TWZ report noted that the imagery could indicate that series production or low-rate initial production has begun. However, the analyst also noted that all four previously identified prototypes could simply have been at the facility at the same time. The TWZ report further analyzed that the KJ-3000 is expected to address longstanding limitations in China's existing large jet-powered AEW&C fleet. When it comes to early models, only four KJ-2000 aircraft have been completed to date. Based on the Russian-built Ilyushin Il-76MD transport, the KJ-2000 program was constrained by the limited availability of suitable airframes. The program now faces the twin issues of reliance on Russian supply chains and aging aircraft. A domestically produced Y-20-based platform provides a more sustainable basis for a much larger AEW&C fleet, with greater scope for upgrades and potentially export opportunities, the report said, noting that the larger airframe should also provide advantages over China's numerous turboprop-powered AEW&C aircraft, including greater speed, range, and endurance. Its higher operating altitude would give its radar a better vantage point for detecting and tracking targets, particularly low-flying aircraft and missiles that may be masked from ground-based sensors by terrain or radar horizon. The aerial refueling probe could further extend the aircraft's range and time on station, although the precise operational capabilities of the KJ-3000 remain unclear. China has not officially announced the existence of the KJ-3000, or its other speculated designation, the KJ-20. However, the development of an early warning variant of the Y-20 large transport aircraft has long been expected by Chinese air force pilots, experts and state media reports. In a documentary on the domestically developed Y-20 large transport aircraft family aired on state broadcaster China Central Television (CCTV) News in August, Pang Rongqi, a member of a Chinese Air Force aviation unit, said, "As a transport aircraft platform, the Y-20 is unique to our country and will play an increasingly important role in the future. The boundaries between transport aircraft and bombers, early warning aircraft, or even electronic warfare aircraft are becoming increasingly blurred. It is possible that all these missions could be accomplished with our transport aircraft platform." Song Zhongping, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times that the Y-20 is China's fully domestically produced large transport aircraft and that it can execute a wide range of combat missions and training support tasks through different combinations of pod modules. Precisely because it is independently manufactured and 100 percent domestically sourced, China enjoys full operational and modification freedom: The Chinese aviation industry and the military can adapt it and employ it in whatever manner they see fit, subject to no external constraints. As long as the relevant technical conditions are met, various military functions can be realized through tailored modification programs. "Since the aircraft was designed and built entirely in-house, it makes the Y-20 an exceptionally suitable base platform: We can mount different pod systems on it to rapidly reconfigure it into a variety of special mission or specialized support aircraft. It can also undergo deeper structural modifications," Song told the Global Times. "For example, by installing a large rotodome on the upper fuselage, it could be converted into a new-generation airborne early warning aircraft." Zhang Junshe, another Chinese military affairs expert, also agreed that the Y-20B transport aircraft possesses strong multi-mission expansion potential and modular conversion capability, allowing it to be quickly converted into a tanker, early warning aircraft or electronic warfare aircraft. Zhang highlighted the significance of the development of the Y-20B based on the original Y-20A, with a perspective on the Y-20's modification potential. He told the Global Times that the most significant upgrade of the Y-20B over the Y-20A is the replacement of engines with the high-bypass-ratio turbofan WS-20. With the WS-20 engines, the Y-20B's cargo capacity and range have been greatly increased. The WS-20 technology is now mature and ready for mass production. On July 6, 2016, the Y-20, China's domestically developed next-generation large military transport aircraft, officially entered service with PLA Air Force aviation units. A decade later, the Y-20 has evolved from a single transport platform into a family of models including the Y-20A, Y-20B and YU-20 aerial refueling tanker, with its operations extending to more than 40 countries and regions across four continents, according to the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, the aircraft's manufacturer, on its WeChat account in June.

item.title: Far-sea capabilities on display as China's 48th naval escort formation completes record Gulf of Aden mission
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-25 21:15:00
The type 052DL destroyer Tangshan (Hull 122) returns to a naval port in Qingdao, East China's Shandong Province, on October 23, 2026. Photo: Screenshot from the PLA Navy WeChat account Cheered by crowds of military and civilian well-wishers lining the pier amid music and flowers, the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Navy's 48th escort taskforce has wrapped up its Gulf of Aden escort mission and returned to Qingdao, East China's Shandong Province. Its 378-day tour at sea stands out as a fresh marker of the service's maturing capacity for sustained far-sea operations, observers and experts say. Made up of the Type 052DL destroyer Tangshan (Hull 122), the Type 054A frigate Daqing (Hull 576), and the Type 903A comprehensive supply ship Taihu (Hull 889), the 48th escort taskforce set sail from Qingdao on October 11, 2025, and returned on Friday morning. The deployment lasted 378 days and covered more than 150,000 nautical miles. The taskforce safely escorted 423 Chinese and foreign vessels, safeguarding international sea lanes and contributing to regional peace and stability. Gulf of Aden escort operations are the PLA Navy's longest-standing and most extensive overseas military practice since its founding, in terms of routine deployment duration, forces employed, and range of activity, safeguarding national strategic interests, said CCTV News. The 48th taskforce's deployment appears to be the longest yet. In recent years, consecutive escort taskforces have each been at sea for about a year, or at least 300 days, longer than earlier rotations, observers noted. Experts said the reliability of Chinese naval equipment and the level of personnel training have reached a high standard, sufficient to sustain long-term, routine far-sea presence. The PLA Navy has also formed a comprehensive support system combining ships' own logistics with overseas support nodes. The Djibouti support base can provide rest and resupply for Gulf of Aden escort formations and is a key element of navy building. Longer deployments, more capability Throughout the mission, the 48th taskforce combined sailing, training, and improvement, using the open ocean as a training ground. It utilized complex maritime environments and organized targeted drills related to escort operations, including armed rescue missions and round-the-clock helicopter flights, enhancing its ability to carry out diversified missions, according to the PLA Navy. Beyond escort duties, the taskforce took part in the "Will for Peace 2026" joint maritime exercise in South Africa and the China-Pakistan "Sea Guardian IV" joint naval exercise in Pakistan. It also took part in a parade marking the 50th anniversary of Seychelles' independence, paid friendly visits to Bangladesh, Myanmar, and Malaysia, and made technical stops in Oman, Kenya, Singapore, and other countries, according to China Military Online. The 378-day voyage is regarded as setting a new record for a single Gulf of Aden escort deployment, said Wang Yunfei, a Chinese military affairs expert. He told the Global Times on Sunday that multiple recent task forces have deployed for noticeably longer than earlier rotations, with three consecutive deployments exceeding 300 days, a clear sign that the PLA Navy's ocean-going adaptability has improved significantly and reached world-class standards. At the foundation is equipment reliability and seaworthiness. Wang said the formation can continue operating without returning to home port for major replenishment, showing that ship maturity and refined logistics have reached a new level. Comprehensive ocean-going replenishment is the core support. Long deployments multiply consumption of fuel, fresh water, food and spare parts. The capability of supply ships, along with choices of replenishment timing and location, directly determines how far and how long a formation can operate. Multiple taskforces sustaining 300-plus days shows coordination between supply ships and combat vessels is highly mature, the expert said. Personnel support is equally critical. A year-long deployment tests the psychology and physiology of officers and sailors. Rotation and rest mechanisms, mental health support and improved living conditions are the soft power that sustains long-term combat capability, Wang said, noting that a taskforce deployment must have all personnel meet the relevant training standards before carrying out missions. Every post must be ready for any task, training, support, navigation, communications, air and missile defense, to sustain long deployments, he noted. Wider support network Beyond the formation itself, the expert said the PLA Navy is gaining more diverse overseas support nodes for far-sea operations. The Djibouti facility plays an irreplaceable role in providing logistics support for Gulf of Aden missions. Separately, the China-Cambodia Joint Support and Training Center at Port Ream represents another regional node within the navy's broader far-sea support architecture. "China's far-sea support combines accompanying logistics with node-based support, enabling sustained operations of nearly a year," Wang said. The Djibouti base is a crucial support facility for the PLA Navy, especially for Gulf of Aden escort taskforces. For escort formations, the base serves as a temporary home and a key support site, allowing for brief shore breaks, ship maintenance and personnel recuperation, Song Zhongping, another Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Sunday. In the future, the PLA may normalize longer periods at sea with occasional shore breaks, which is a humane consideration and an important way to further boost combat power. Port calls for fresh food, routine supplies, fresh water and other daily necessities all help improve combat readiness, Song said. Ships carrying Chinese military personnel departed Zhanjiang in South China's Guangdong Province on July 11, 2017, to set up a support base in Djibouti. The establishment of the PLA Djibouti base was a decision made by the two countries, according to the PLA Navy. The Ream support and training center can also support PLA overseas humanitarian and disaster relief operations and play a positive role in regional security affairs, Song added. The Cambodia-China Joint Support and Training Center at Port Ream started operating in April, 2025, according to the Xinhua News Agency. At the ceremony at the time, the Chinese and Cambodian sides emphasized that the construction and operation of the center were the result of mutual respect and equal consultation between China and Cambodia, which is conducive to further strengthening ties between the two militaries, better fulfilling international obligations and providing international public security products. Ship support alone is point support; adding comprehensive supply ships creates line support; adding training and support bases creates a point-line-plane integrated support system, Song noted. Strengthening this capability will greatly lift the PLA's capacity to undertake international maritime missions and support its blue‑water navy development. According to CCTV, in 2008, severe pirate hijackings occurred in the Gulf of Aden. On December 26, 2008, the PLA Navy's Type 052B destroyer Wuhan (Hull 169), Type 052C destroyer Haikou (Hull 171) and comprehensive supply ship Weishanhu (Hull 887) formed the first escort taskforce and set sail from a naval port in Sanya, South China's Hainan Province, opening China's naval escort operations in the Gulf of Aden and waters off Somalia. In recent years, pirate attacks in the Gulf of Aden and off Somalia have declined, indicating that the deterrence efforts of the PLA Navy, along with other international forces, and the joint endeavors of escort task forces, have been effective. From counter-piracy information sharing and commanders' exchanges on board ships to joint escorts, joint exercises and the embarkation of exchange officers for observation, the PLA Navy has engaged in cooperation with many countries and international organizations. This demonstrates an open, confident and cooperative posture, reflecting China's sincerity and commitment to contributing to world peace and security.

item.title: China-Pakistan drill features Type 08 IFV with roof cage, grilles
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 22:36:00
A Type 08 infantry fighting vehicle fitted with a roof cage and side grilles drives down a road during the China-Pakistan Karakoram 2026 joint army training in Korla, Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. Photo: Screenshot from the CCTV News The ongoing China-Pakistan Karakoram 2026 joint army training exercise in Korla, Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, has moved into its segmented drill phase, with mixed units completing a full reconnaissance, strike and clearance sequence, CCTV News reported on Wednesday. Highlights of the report include footage of a Chinese Type 08 infantry fighting vehicle (IFV) fitted with a roof cage and side grilles, alongside drone swarms and robot dogs deployed in live drills. A Chinese expert said such adaptations reflect lessons drawn from real combat. Over the past few days, Chinese and Pakistani troops have moved into the segmented phase, which involves missions ranging from air-ground reconnaissance and concentrated fire strikes to search and clearance, with mixed units completing multiple tactical actions and honing joint counter-terrorism skills, reported CCTV. At the start of the drill, reconnaissance vehicles and drones deployed simultaneously to monitor targets inside the camp, tracking the terrorists' force disposition and movements in real time. Once intelligence was gathered, the fire strike phase began immediately. Snipers seized vantage points for long-range kills. Drone swarms launched suicide strikes on exposed targets, while ground armor fire followed to ensure full coverage. The Type 08 IFV then carried the assault team forward, a signal that the fire strike phase had ended, said CCTV. Notably, the vehicle's roof was fitted with a metal grille, with grilles also added to its sides, specifically designed to counter drone attacks. The roof cage on the Type 08 is a rapid tactical adaptation to drone threats, Song Zhongping, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Wednesday. The Russia-Ukraine and Middle East conflicts have shown militaries worldwide just how serious that threat has become. Adding roof protection to armored vehicles is a direct response, drawing on battlefield lessons to improve equipment performance. According to Military Watch Magazine on September 12, the Russia-Ukraine conflict has substantially altered the configuration of Russian tanks. First-person view drones and other unmanned systems have made the upper surfaces, rear sections and engine compartments of tanks particularly vulnerable, with vehicles having consequently appeared with increasingly elaborate roof protection, additional armor and electronic warfare equipment intended to interfere with drone attacks. Earlier, in November 2025, the Xinhua News Agency cited a report from German news channel n-tv that said to better protect vehicles from suicide drone attacks, Russian forces have continued to develop new countermeasures. After the introduction of improvised "turtle shell" and "porcupine" armor, photos of a novel device have circulated on social media, with military bloggers calling it the "hedgehog tank" based on its appearance. Returning to the China-Pakistan drill, CCTV reported that once the IFV reached its position, assault troops dismounted immediately and moved into the terrorist camp, followed by several more Type 08s carrying clearance teams. As soon as they stopped, the troops dismounted. Their mission is to push deeper into the camp to eliminate remaining terrorists. These troops coordinated with robot dogs, which scouted building interiors ahead of them, reducing the risk of casualties. Song noted that this joint training exercise is themed on joint counter-terrorism and clearance operations in high-altitude areas. However, even during counter-terrorism drills, plateau units make full use of asymmetric assets like drones. Terrorist groups also might use drones for sabotage operations, and the PLA must have sufficient means to counter the threat and challenges posed by these drones. In high-altitude environments, drones and counter-drone tactics might see new approaches, and a set of drone and counter-drone tactics suited to plateau terrain needs to be developed. Realistic drills are essential to solidifying tactics and training, Song said. The report noted that despite the language barrier, days of continuous skill training have built tactical chemistry among the mixed teams. "What impressed me most about this joint training is that the Pakistani military has real combat experience, so many of their lessons are worth learning. When we enter a building and throw a grenade, we throw it far; they throw it at the ground so it bounces at speed, ricocheting two or three times instead of staying in one place. That effectively stops the enemy from picking it up and throwing it back," Pan Li, a member of a unit under the Xinjiang military command, was quoted by CCTV as saying. Through days of training, the two sides have learned from each other's tactics, shared combat experience and further refined their skills, effectively improving joint counter-terrorism capabilities, the report said. On October 10, Senior Colonel Chen Xi, a spokesperson for the Chinese Ministry of National Defense, announced that in mid and late October, Chinese and Pakistani armies will hold Karakoram 2026 joint army training in Korla, Xinjiang region. Focusing on joint counter-terrorism operations in high-altitude areas, the activity will include skill training in UAV operation, on-the-move target search and firing, and long-range sniping, as well as cover joint command and live-force exercises. This is the first joint army training to be carried out by the two countries, which will help the two sides deepen cooperation and strengthen interoperability in counter-terrorism. On October 14, CCTV Military channel emphasized in a report that all weapons and equipment were provided by China, including Type 191 rifles, Type 201 squad machine guns, Type 11 armored assault vehicles, Type 08 infantry fighting vehicles, as well as artillery, unmanned and anti-unmanned systems.

item.title: China permits, monitors Philippine resupply to illegally grounded vessel at Ren'ai Jiao: CCG spokesperson

item.title: Chinese expert calls Japan's six reports on PLA activities over two days sensationalism aimed at justifying own military buildup
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-20 22:31:00
The Type 901 sea-going comprehensive replenishment ship Hulunhu (Hull 901) conducts an underway replenishment drill. Photo: China Military Online Japan's Defense Ministry issued six consecutive reports on Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) ship and aircraft movements on Monday and Tuesday, covering the 48th escort task group, a supply ship, electronic reconnaissance vessels and reconnaissance aircraft. A military expert said that, with the Liaoning carrier group training in the far seas and the large US-Japan "Keen Sword 27" exercise underway, the frequent disclosures amount to alarmism aimed at justifying Japan's military buildup. On Tuesday, the ministry claimed the PLA Navy's Type 054A guided-missile frigate Jingzhou (Hull 532) had transited the Osumi Strait toward the Pacific on Monday. Monday's five reports included one claiming that on Saturday, the PLA Navy's Type 052D destroyer Tangshan (Hull 122), Type 054A frigate Daqing (Hull 576) and Type 903A comprehensive supply ship Taihu (Hull 889) passed through the Miyako Strait into the East China Sea. These vessels make up the PLA 48th escort task group, which set sail on October 11, 2025, and handed over duties to the 49th task force on September 7, according to reports from state media outlets. The group has not yet returned home, meaning the deployment has now exceeded a year. The Japanese ministry also claimed on Monday that the Type 052D destroyer Qiqihar (Hull 121) and the Type 901 sea-going comprehensive replenishment ship Hulunhu (Hull 901) transited the Osumi Strait into the Western Pacific on Saturday. Two other notices claimed the PLA Navy's electronic reconnaissance ship 796 entered the Western Pacific through the Miyako Strait on Saturday, while electronic reconnaissance ship 798 passed through the Osumi Strait into the Western Pacific between Saturday and Sunday. A fifth notice said that on Monday, a PLA BZK-005 reconnaissance drone and a Y-9 intelligence-gathering aircraft flew from the East China Sea through the Miyako Strait into the Pacific, circled over the ocean and returned. The same day, a PLA TB-001 reconnaissance/strike drone flew from the East China Sea through the area between Yonaguni Island and Taiwan island into the Pacific. Zhang Junshe, a Chinese military affairs expert, offered his analysis of the reports. The Hulunhu is a new-generation comprehensive supply ship independently developed by China to world-class standards, capable of providing underway replenishment for carrier groups and far-sea maneuver formations, Zhang told the Global Times. A carrier group typically consists of an aircraft carrier, destroyers, frigates, logistics support ships and a nuclear submarine. Japan had already released reports on two Type 055 destroyers and a Type 052D, and has now added a large comprehensive supply ship. This likely means the Hulunhu could subsequently join the Liaoning carrier group conducting far-sea training in the Western Pacific. The PLA Navy sent the Liaoning carrier task group to the Western Pacific on October 14 for training, the PLA Navy said in a statement. This is the Liaoning 's second far-sea training deployment to the Western Pacific this year, which also marks the 10th anniversary of its first such deployment in late December 2016, more than four years after the carrier entered service. The Hulunhu can quickly conduct both alongside and vertical replenishment of large volumes of supplies with high efficiency, supporting carrier operations far from shore. If it joined the Liaoning group, the formation would gain sustained training and extended far-sea presence without port calls, enabling longer exercises and more complex drills, and improving the carrier group's ocean-going endurance, presence and combat capability, Zhang said. Meanwhile, a large US-Japan exercise is currently underway. The US and Japan were set to launch the large-scale "Keen Sword 27" military exercise, involving more than 50,000 personnel from the SDF and US forces, on Monday, the Kyodo News reported on Saturday. Against the backdrop of the Liaoning 's far-sea training and the US-Japan drills, Zhang said, the Chinese reconnaissance aircraft and ships could provide situational awareness and intelligence support for the carrier group to a certain extent. This multi-layered reconnaissance setup reflects the PLA Navy's approach to system-based far-sea training and joint operations. First, it builds a far-sea comprehensive support and situational awareness system, improving the carrier group's sustained combat capability and information advantage in complex waters far from base. Second, complementary reconnaissance platforms enable three-dimensional, real-time battlefield awareness, improving information acquisition and responsiveness in complex electromagnetic environments and high-intensity confrontations. Third, it tests and improves system-based combat effectiveness in realistic conditions, reflecting a combat-oriented training approach, the expert explained. Zhang noted Japan's frequent releases of PLA ship and aircraft movements, sometimes multiple notices in a single day, amount to making a fuss out of nothing. During past training, Chinese naval formations have consistently handled tracking, surveillance and harassment by foreign parties, especially Japan, in accordance with laws and regulations. The Western Pacific is not any country's backyard, and international waterways are not anyone's doorstep. Additionally, Japan's sensationalism cannot hinder the normal development of China's national defense, Zhang added.

item.title: Chinese PLA forces track, monitor USS Charleston after illegal intrusion into waters adjacent to China's Xianbin Jiao
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-20 13:32:00
This photo carried in a report named "A Survey Report on the Coral Reef Ecosystem of Xianbin Jiao" shows an aerial view of Xianbin Jiao of China's Nansha Qundao. Photo: Xinhua In the early hours of Tuesday, the US littoral combat ship USS Charleston illegally intruded into the waters adjacent to Xianbin Jiao of China's Nansha Qundao without approval from the Chinese government. The People's Liberation Army (PLA) Southern Theater Command Navy dispatched forces to track and monitor the US vessel in accordance with laws and regulations, Yin Gang, a spokesperson for the PLA Southern Theater Command Navy, said in a statement on Tuesday. China holds indisputable sovereignty over Nansha Qundao and its adjacent waters. The US action infringes upon China's sovereign rights and interests, jeopardizes maritime security, and is detrimental to regional peace and stability. The US side should immediately cease such activities, Yin said. Forces of the Southern Theater Command remain on high alert at all times to resolutely safeguard national sovereignty and security and uphold regional peace and stability, said the spokesperson. Xianbin Jiao lies in the southeastern waters of China's Nansha Qundao, and its position along several international shipping lanes gives it significant strategic importance. The US littoral combat ship's close-in provocation there is a calculated move driven by the area's geostrategic value and other considerations, Zhang Junshe, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Tuesday. Through such calculated provocations, the US seeks to test China's red lines on maritime passage and regional control while obstructing China's law enforcement and sovereignty protection efforts around the shoal. This deliberately challenges China's sovereignty in the South China Sea and undermines regional peace under the guise of so-called "freedom of navigation," said Zhang. Compared with previous US military operations conducted under the banner of "freedom of navigation," those near Xianbin Jiao have been relatively rare. Yet this latest move suggests that US policy toward the South China Sea remains fundamentally unchanged and that China-US competition in these waters continues. The operation also aims to signal support for the Philippines and underscore the US military presence in the South China Sea, Chen Xiangmiao, a research fellow at the National Institute for South China Sea Studies, told the Global Times. Xianbin Jiao has been a flashpoint in China Philippines maritime frictions in recent years. For example, in September, a Philippine vessel caused a collision with a China Coast Guard (CCG) boat near Xianbin Jiao in China's Nansha Qundao after ignoring repeated warnings and cutting across its bow, Jiang Lue, a spokesperson for the CCG, said in a statement. Jiang also sternly warned the Philippine side to immediately stop all acts of infringement and provocation, or bear all consequences arising from them. Zhang noted that Philippine coast guard vessels have repeatedly intruded illegally into waters around Xianbin Jiao and staged beaching provocations, seeking to create a fact on the ground to assert Manila's so-called "sovereignty." By dispatching warships for close-in provocations at this juncture, the US also aims to provide military backing for Manila's risky moves, tie down China's navy and coast guard, and raise China's maritime governance costs while maximizing disruption at minimal cost. China's swift public response to the US littoral combat ship's incursion into waters around Xianbin Jiao underscores its resolve to defend national sovereignty, territorial integrity, and maritime rights and interests. It also demonstrates the Chinese military's vigilance and readiness to counter security threats, sending a clear message: China will brook no compromise on these core interests, said Zhang. The prompt official statement following the early-morning incident highlights China's round-the-clock surveillance and rapid-response capabilities in the South China Sea. "Unauthorized intrusions that infringe upon China's rights can be detected, tracked and addressed without delay," said the expert.
